fixes.explanation: Close, but that's not what Pharaoh says. He doesn't give anybody else a thank-you. He says, "The Nile is mine; I made it myself." (Ezekiel 29:3) Nobody else gets a mention in that sentence.

God says it plainly: "I will haul you up out of your rivers, and all the fish of your streams will cling to your scales." (Ezekiel 29:4) So the fish come along for the ride. Nobody asked those fish if they wanted to go. I think they had a rough trip.

I can see why a comeback story sounds nice, but God says no. He says, "Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations." (Ezekiel 29:15) He adds, "For I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations." (Ezekiel 29:15) That one stays False, friend.

Right, False. God says Egypt "…will never again exalt itself above the nations." and adds, "…I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations." (Ezekiel 29:15) Egypt does get to come home to Pathros, where "…they will be a lowly kingdom." (Ezekiel 29:14) It gets to come home, but not to the top.

Years of slavery are a heavy memory, but this verse points somewhere else. God says Egypt "…will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians." (Ezekiel 29:16) The reminder is about turning to Egypt.
The Red Sea doesn't come up in this passage. God says Egypt "…will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians." (Ezekiel 29:16) That's the memory He names.

Right, False. The text says Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his army "…received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it." (Ezekiel 29:18) Tyre is the city they worked against. That's a lot of hard work with nothing in the envelope.
